cases.note: A path with a value exists.
Zero is a value. A robot at 0% has reported its battery.
An explicit null does not exist — somebody looked and found nothing.
An empty list does not exist. No guards active is not "guards".
A string of spaces does not exist.
The escape hatch: `exists` is the one operator an absent path does not refuse. It answers unsatisfied, so `not(exists(p))` still means what its author meant.
The ordinary case.
A different value.
A literal null equals an explicit null: both are primitives.

A literal array in a rule is never equal to anything. `===` on two objects is reference equality, and a rule's literal was never the context's object. `includes` is the operator for this intent, and finding that out here is cheaper than finding it out in a cell.
Two operands read from the same path are one object, so they are equal even though neither is a primitive. This is the only way an object comparison can hold.
Two arrays with identical contents at different paths are not equal, because `===` is not a deep comparison. `skill.also` holds exactly what `skill.needs` holds.
A path may address an array member, and the member is the same object the collection holds.
Not in estop.
It is idle, so it is not not-idle.

The headline change. `neq` against a path that names nothing used to answer **true** — `undefined !== "estop"` — so a rule reading "the robot is not in estop" passed on a robot that had never reported a mode. It now refuses and names the path.
The value is one of the listed.
The value is not.
A non-array right-hand side is wrapped.
The collection contains the rule's value.
It does not.
Every capability the skill needs is present.
One is missing.
An empty requirement is vacuously satisfied: nothing was asked for. This is now reachable only from a requirement that *is* empty, never from one nobody could read.

The rule this module's own documentation uses as its example — "robot capabilities must cover whatever this policy declares" — used to **pass** when the policy declared nothing readable, because `every` over an empty list is true. It now refuses and names the reference.
At least one.
None of them.
Nothing was asked for.
Battery above reserve.
And the same fact from the other side.
Strictly greater is not greater-or-equal.
And the boundary itself.
A percentage reported as a string still compares. Robots report numbers as strings, and an edition that refused this one and accepted the next would be a robot that stops for a quote.
A decimal string.
`Number("0x1f")` is 31, and this is the reference being mirrored rather than a shape anybody should write.
`Number("1e3")` is 1000.
`Number("Infinity")` is not finite, and a ceiling nothing can exceed is not a comparison.
A fixture name is not a number.
A blank string is not zero here.
A boolean is not coerced. `Number(true)` is 1 in JavaScript and the reference never reaches it: only numbers and strings are read.
An explicit null is present and is not a number.
The reference names the side that failed, and here it is the rule's own reference rather than the robot's value.
The runtime is inside the skill's window.
And outside a different one.
A wildcard constrains nothing and is a valid range.
A version this edition cannot parse is a fact about the declaration, not a version that fell outside the window — so it is named rather than counted as a miss.
And the same for the range.

Stricter than `satisfies`, deliberately: `>=1.0.0 || garbage` is satisfied by 1.4.2 and is still a range half of which nobody can read. A skill whose window is half unreadable is a skill whose publisher has to hear about it, so the operator refuses where the function would not.
The ordinary conjunction.
A conjunction whose first child is false stops there, so the refusal names a predicate that was actually false rather than the unreadable one behind it.
And when the unreadable one comes first, that is what is named. Which predicate a refusal names must not depend on how an edition iterates.
A skill declaring no preconditions is not a skill that fails them.
An alternative that holds ends the question; the unreadable one beside it never mattered.
With nothing holding, a disjunction containing something unreadable is not known to be false — only unread.
No alternatives, nothing holds.
Negation of a decided answer is a decided answer.

The change that matters most. `not(eq(robot.state.mode, "estop"))` over a robot that has never reported a mode used to be **true**, because `!false` is true and `undefined === "estop"` is false. Ignorance does not negate into knowledge.
And the idiom this must not break: `exists` answers about absence, so negating it is meaningful.
The first child of `predicates` is accepted as the operand.
A `not` with nothing to negate used to answer **true** — `!evaluate(undefined)` — which is a malformed rule passing.
An array member is addressed by its index.
Past the end is nothing.
Not a canonical index, and therefore not a member. JavaScript agrees: `["a"]["01"]` is undefined.

`length` is a property of a JavaScript array and not a member of the document, so it does not resolve. An edition without JavaScript arrays could not reproduce it, and a path vocabulary one edition can read is not a path vocabulary.
Nor is anything else off the prototype chain. Rules are operator-supplied rows, and a path they compose has no business reaching `constructor`.
A path cannot continue through a string.
Nor through an explicit null.
An empty segment names no member.
A predicate with no path cannot read anything.

A `path` that is not a string used to reach `path.split` and **throw**, taking the whole compatibility check down with one bad rule row — in a module whose first paragraph says it is total. It is read defensively now.
An empty path is no path.
`{ path: … }` is accepted as an alias for `__ref`.
With a second key it is an object literal, not a reference — and an object literal is never equal to anything, so this asks whether the capability list contains an object.
A reference that names nothing refuses, and the refusal names the reference rather than the left-hand path.
A null predicate is not a predicate.
Nor is a number.
Nor is an object with no operator.
Nor one whose operator is not a string.
An operator this edition does not implement is named, not guessed at.

A `predicates` that is not an array used to reach `.every` and throw. It is malformed — deliberately not "no children", because a conjunction over no children is *satisfied*, and turning a broken rule into a pass is the failure this whole change is about.
What a `SkillManifest` precondition becomes: the guards that must be running, the calibration that must be valid, the battery that must be above reserve, the cell that must be closed.
The same tree against the set that expired. §45 makes a lapsed calibration a fact rather than a warning, and this is where that fact stops a skill.

And the one §54.2 exists for: a precondition naming something this robot does not expose is refused with the path named, so the answer is "nobody declared a payload" rather than "the payload is wrong".
